sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
[p. B-1] This appendix provides worked design examples for bridge foundation support on shallow foundations in several applications using Service Load Design (SLD) methodology. The applications and design considerations for each are discussed briefly below. The examples follow the design process outlined in Table 6-1 and shown in the flow chart in Figure 6-1.

It should be noted that these examples are intended to convey one approach and process that can lead to a satisfactory design of bridge support on a shallow foundation. The examples should not be construed as representations of the only approach that can lead to a satisfactory design. Also note that the examples only check one or, at most, a few specific load cases. In practice, every complete design should consider all applicable load cases.

EXAMPLE 1: INTERIOR BRIDGE PIER ON A SPREAD FOOTING FOUNDED IN NATIVE SOIL

This example uses SLD Group I loads from service load design of an interior bridge column. The purpose of the example is to show how bearing capacity and settlement are considered together to calculate an allowable bearing capacity that controls the design of the footing.

EXAMPLE 2: INTEGRAL STUB ABUTMENT ON COMPACTED STRUCTURAL FILL

This example shows the successful and cost-effective application of a spread footing at a structurally integral abutment supported in a compacted structural fill over good foundation conditions. Since integral abutments are most frequently supported on pile foundations, this example was developed to illustrate the feasibility of using a spread footing in lieu of piles in order to realize the cost savings potential of shallow foundations. The load case is SLD Group I.

EXAMPLE 3: STUB SEAT-TYPE ABUTMENT FOOTING IN COMPACTED STRUCTURAL FILL

This example uses SLD Group IV loads to show the effect of shear loads transmitted through the bearing pads due to temperature and shrinkage, etc., at a seat-type abutment with a joint. The example also shows the effective use of engineered embankment design and stage construction to permit the use of a spread footing supported in an approach fill over embankment foundation conditions that are less than excellent.

[p. B-2] EXAMPLE 4: FULL-HEIGHT SEAT ABUTMENT FOUNDED IN NATIVE SOIL

This example shows the design of a tall abutment founded on a spread footing in good ground conditions. The load case is SLD Group I. The example also shows design of a concrete cantilever retaining wall, since the intermediate construction stage of a backfilled stem without superstructure loads is also checked.

EXAMPLE 5: INTERIOR BRIDGE PIER ON A SPREAD FOOTING ON NATIVE ROCK

This example uses excellent foundation conditions and Group VII seismic loads to show an example of foundation design governed by considerations other than bearing capacity or settlement.

Note: Unless cited with a specific reference (e.g., AASHTO, 1996), the equation numbers in the examples refer to those in the main body of this Circular.

sections.title: Example 1: Interior Bridge Pier on Spread Footing
sections.body:

• Subsurface profile at the interior bridge pier is shown in Figure B1-1.

• There is no scour potential at this site.

• Frost penetration depth is 0.6 m (2 ft).

• Tolerable settlement is 38 mm (1.5 in).

• The sign conventions and loading directions are shown in Figure B1-2.

Find:

• Size the footing based on AASHTO Service Load Design, Group I loads (allowable stress design method) considering both the settlement and bearing capacity. Check for overturning and sliding.

[p. B-4] Solution:

The solution can be obtained by following the step-by-step process shown in Figure 6-1, Design Process Flow Chart.

sections.title: Example 1, Step 5 – Determine the loads applied to the footing
sections.body:
[p. B-4] The structural engineer has calculated and provided the values shown in Table B1-1.

[p. B-5] [Table B1-1]

Service Load Design Loads for Group I:

The general equation is:

PI = γ [βD(D) + βL (L + I) + βC(CF) + βE(E) + βB (B) + βS(SF) + βW(W) + βWL(WL) + βL(LF) + βR(R + S + T) + βEQ(EQ) + βICE(ICE)] (AASHTO, 1996, Eqn. 3-10)

where: γ = Load factor (always equal to 1.0 for SLD)

βi = Coefficient for particular load, i, as found in Table 3.22.1A of AASHTO (1996).

Recall from Table 6-2, that SLD Group I is the load combination for normal vehicles using the bridge without wind, and that earthquake loads are only considered in Load Group VII. Therefore the coefficients for W, WL and EQ are all zero and the general load equation reduces to the following for this example:

PI = γ [βD(D) + βL (L + I)]

The AASHTO provisions permit neglecting the impact load, I, for foundations and buried structures. Also, since the footing is relatively shallow, assume that the effect of footing self-weight is negligible. The factored loads are as follows:

Axial Loads:

PI = γ [βD(D) + βL (L)] = 1.0 [1.0 (6400 kN) + 1.0 (1670 kN)] = 8070 kN

[p. B-6] Shear:

V = γ[βD (D) + βL (L)] = 1.0 [1.0 (167 kN) + 1.0 (42 kN)] = 209 kN

Moment in the Z direction:

MZ = γ[βD (D) + βL (L)] = 1.0 [1.0 (211 kN-m) + 1.0 (409 kN-m)] = 620 kN-m

Moment in the Y direction:

MY = γ[βD (D) + βL (L + I)] = 1.0 [1.0 (748 kN-m) + 1.0 (196.5 kN-m)] = 944.5 kN-m (as printed; the numbers take L alone, 196.5 kN-m, the impact load being neglected)

sections.title: Example 1, Step 7 – Calculate allowable bearing capacity
sections.body:
[p. B-7] The geotechnical engineer will calculate the allowable bearing capacity, considering both the potential for bearing capacity failure (Section 5.1) and settlement (Section 5.2) (as printed; settlement estimation is Section 5.3).

Calculate ultimate bearing capacity:

The general equation for bearing capacity is:

qult = cNcscbc + qNqCWqsqbqdq + 0.5γBfNγCWγsγbγ (Eqn. 5-14)

[p. B-8] The first term goes to zero since the foundation materials are granular and cohesionless, so the cohesion term, c, is zero.

For the interior pier, we will assume that the footing is essentially rectangular (L/B < 5). Recall that the shape and inclination factors should not be applied together (see discussion in Section 5.2). Since the effect of the shape factors is significant for rectangular footings, and the inclination resulting from the relatively small shear load component (V) is small, we will only apply the shape factors as follows:

sγ = 1 - 0.4 Bf/Lf (Table 5-2). Assume the effect of eccentricity is small for now, so Bf ≅ Lf

sγ = 0.6

A design friction angle associated with Layer 2 is needed to calculate sq. The geotechnical engineer has recommended that the footing be cast against the firm, undisturbed soil of Unit 2. Unit 2 is 2.1-m thick and overlies denser material at depth, so the properties of Unit 2 will govern the footing design. From Figure B1-1, the average uncorrected field SPT N-value for this layer is 20. From Figure B1-3, the average vertical effective stress in Layer 2 is 65.7 kPa (about 1.4 ksf). Entering Figure 4-1 with a blowcount of 20 and a vertical effective stress of 1.4 ksf, a relative density, DR, of about 75 percent is read. Entering Figure 4-2 with this relative density for silty sand (Unified Soil Classification ‘SM’), a friction angle of 35 is selected for computing bearing capacity.

sq = 1 + (Bf/Lf) tan φ (Table 5-2)

sq = 1 + (1/1) tan(35°)

sq = 1.7

Since the overburden materials above the footing are cohesive soils, the correction factor to account for shearing resistance of the material above the bearing elevation, dq, should be set equal to 1.0:

dq = 1.0 (Table 5-4)

Since this footing will be level, there is no effect of inclination of the base, so:

bγ = bq = 1.0 (Table 5-5)

Calculate the effect of the footing embedment, q. Apply judgment and recognize that it is minimal excavation to remove all of the Unit 1 medium stiff lean clay and avoid any associated low strength or compressibility characteristics in this material. Therefore select Df = 2.3 m to bear below Unit 1:

[p. B-9] In this case q is only a function of the depth of bearing.

q = σ'vo = γ'Df where: γ' = γbulk = 19.6 kN/m³

q = (19.6 kN/m³)(2.3 m)

q = 45.1 kPa

Check ground water effect:

Depth of ground water table below the bearing depth:

Df = Depth of footing = 2.3 m. Assumes a 0.9-m thick footing and 1.4-m cover

Dw = Depth of ground water below the ground surface (Df ) = 9.1 m

Conservatively estimate the footing width with an upper bound value of Bf = 6 m.

Calculate ground water correction factors, CWγ and CWq:

CWγ = 0.5 + 0.5 (DW / (1.5Bf + Df)) ≤ 1.0 (Eqn. 5-10) (as printed; this is Eqn. 5-9, p. 56)

CWγ = 0.5 + 0.5 (9.1 / (1.5(6) + 2.3)) = 0.9

CWq = 0.5 + 0.5 (DW / Df) ≤ 1.0 (Eqn. 5-11) (as printed; this is Eqn. 5-10, p. 56)

CWq = 0.5 + 0.5 (9.1 / 2.3) = 2.48 ; Use CWq = 1.0

From Table 5-1, the bearing capacity factors, Nγ and Nq, are 48.0 and 33.3, respectively, for a friction angle of 35 degrees in Layer 2.

So the equation for bearing capacity is:

qult = qNqCWqsqbqdq + 0.5γBfNγCWγsγbγ

qult = 45.1 kPa (33.3)(1.0)(1.7)(1.0)(1.0) + 0.5 (19.6 kN/m³)(Bf)(48.0)(0.9)(0.6)(1.0)

qult = 2553 kPa + 254Bf

[p. B-10] Incorporating a factor of safety of 3.0:

qall = qult ÷ 3.0

qall = (2553 kPa + 254Bf) ÷ 3.0

qall = 851 + 85Bf kPa

Estimate Footing Settlement

Calculate stress increase at the midpoint of each soil layer using the 2-on-1 stress distribution method for various footing widths – say, Bf = 3, 4.6 and 6.1 m:

ΔσV/q = (Bf)(Lf) / ((Bf + Z)(Lf + Z)) (Figure 5-12)

but Bf ≅ Lf, so:

ΔσV/q = Bf² / (Bf + Z)²

Layer 2 with midpoint of layer @ Z = 1.05 m below base of footing:

ΔσV2/q = 3² / (3 + 1.05)² = 0.55

Layer 3a with midpoint of layer @ Z = 4.45 m below base of footing:

ΔσV3a/q = 3² / (3 + 4.45)² = 0.16

Layer 3b with midpoint of layer @ Z = 8.3 m below base of footing:

ΔσV3b/q = 3² / (3 + 8.3)² = 0.07

Layer 4 with midpoint of layer @ Z = 11.3 m below base of footing:

ΔσV4/q = 3² / (3 + 11.3)² = 0.04

Perform similar calculations for Bf = 4.6 m and Bf = 6.1 m and tabulate:

[p. B-11] [Table B1-2]

Determine stress applied by footing to generate 38 mm of settlement for same range of footing widths, Bf = 3, 4.6 and 6.1 m, using the Hough method:

General equation:

ΔH = Ho (1/C′) log((σ′vo + Δσvf) / σ′vo) (Eqn. 5-24)

Correct SPT blowcounts to account for overburden pressure, N′, for each layer, and enter Figure 5-19 to obtain bearing capacity factor, C′:

Layer 2: Navg = 20; N′/N = 1.2 (from Figure 5-18); N′ = 24; C′ = 65 (from Figure 5-19 for silty Sand)

Layer 3a: Navg = 40; N′/N = 0.9 (from Figure 5-18); N′ = 36; C′ = 120 (from Figure 5-19 for well-graded Sand and Gravel)

Layer 3b: Navg = 43; N′/N = 0.7 (from Figure 5-18); N′ = 30; C′ = 102 (from Figure 5-19 for well-graded Sand and Gravel)

Layer 4: Navg = 40; N′/N = 0.66 (from Figure 5-18); N′ = 26; C′ = 110 (from Figure 5-19 for clean, uniform Sand)

[p. B-12] Calculate settlement in each layer and sum the settlements to obtain the total settlement for a range of applied stresses and footing widths. Select applied stresses of q = 240 kPa, 290 kPa, 335 kPa and 380 kPa (corresponding to about 3, 4, 5 and 6 ksf) and nominal footing widths of 3, 4.6 and 6.1 m:

Layer 2 (Bf = 3 m):

ΔH2 = H2(1/C') log[(σ'vo + Δσv)/σ'vo]

ΔH2 = 2.1 m (1/65) log[(65.7 kPa + 0.55(240 kPa))/65.7 kPa]

ΔH2 = 0.015 m = 15 mm

ΔH3a = H3a(1/C') log[(σ'vo + Δσv)/σ'vo]

ΔH3a = 4.7 m (1/120) log[(132 kPa + 0.16(240 kPa))/132 kPa]

ΔH3a = 0.004 m = 4 mm

ΔH3b = H3(1/C') log[(σ'vo + Δσv)/σ'vo]

ΔH3b = 3.0 m (1/102) log[(193 kPa + 0.07(240 kPa))/193 kPa]

ΔH3b = 0.001 m = 1 mm

ΔH4 = H4(1/C') log[(σ'vo + Δσv)/σ'vo]

ΔH4 = 3 m (1/110) log[(222 kPa + 0.04(240 kPa))/222 kPa]

ΔH4 = 0.0005 m ≅ 1 mm

ΣΔHi = 15 mm + 4 mm + 1 mm + 1 mm = 21 mm

Repeat and tabulate for various footing widths and applied stresses (a spreadsheet or computer tool can make these calculations rapidly):

[Table B1-3]

[p. B-13] Compare to allowable bearing capacities at same footing widths relative to shear failure, remembering that the maximum tolerable settlement is 38 mm:

For Bf = 3 m:

qall = 851 + 85(3 m) kPa = 1106 kPa >> 380 kPa (with 30 mm settlement)

For Bf = 4.6 m:

qall = 851 + 85(4.6 m) kPa = 1242 kPa >> 335 kPa (with 34 mm settlement)

For Bf = 6.1 m:

qall = 851 + 85(6.1 m) kPa = 1369 kPa >> 290 kPa (with 35 mm settlement)

Settlement will therefore limit the allowable bearing capacity for the design of this footing. Interpolating the values in Table B1-3, find ranges of footing widths that will limit settlement to 38 mm or less at allowable bearing capacities of 335 kPa and 380 kPa as shown in Table B1-4.

[Table B1-4]

The geotechnical engineer should provide this table to the structural designer for sizing of the footing.

sections.title: Example 1, Step 8 – Calculate sliding and passive soil resistance
sections.body:
[p. B-13] The footing will bear in the Unit 2 soils. The friction angle, φ, of 35 degrees selected in Step 7 will be used to compute sliding resistance.

The general equation for sliding resistance on cohesionless soils is:

FR = (W + Pv) tan δ (Eqn. 5-38)

The second term goes to zero since we are founding the footing on a cohesionless soil unit. For a concrete footing cast against the ground, δ = φ, so the ultimate sliding resistance is:

FR = (W + Pv) tan 35° = 0.7(W + Pv)

[p. B-14] Since the sliding resistance will develop at strain levels much lower than those needed to develop passive pressures against the side of the footing, passive pressure will be ignored unless it is found that sliding resistance governs the design of the footing. The geotechnical engineer should provide this equation and the assumptions regarding use of passive pressures to the structural engineer for checking the footing’s resistance to sliding.

sections.title: Example 1, Step 10 – Size the footing
sections.body:
[p. B-14] The structural designer should make a preliminary estimate of the size of the footing by dividing the Group I axial load by the largest allowable bearing pressure from Table B1-4:

A = PI ÷ qall

A = 8070 kN ÷ 380 kPa = 21.2 m²

Bf = Lf = √A ≅ 4.6 m

Then calculate eccentricity and effective footing dimensions:

B′f = Bf - 2ey (Eqn. 6-6)

ey = MZ ÷ P

ey = 620 kN-m ÷ 8070 kN = 0.077 m

B′f = 4.6 m - 2(0.077 m) = 4.45 m

L′f = Lf - 2ez (Eqn. 6-7)

ez = MY ÷ P

ez = 944.5 kN-m ÷ 8070 k (as printed, for kN) = 0.117 m

L′f = 4.6 m - 2(0.117 m) = 4.37 m

A′ = B′f · L′f = (4.45 m)(4.37 m) = 19.4 m²

Check allowable bearing stress for effective footing area:

qapplied = P ÷ A′ = 8070 kN ÷ 19.4 m² = 416 kPa

This is greater than qall = 380 kPa for footings less than 5.0 m wide, according to Table B1-4, in order to limit settlement to less than 38 mm. Therefore the footing should be sized larger.

[p. B-15] Try a 4.9 m-by-4.9 m footing. Calculate eccentricity and effective footing dimensions:

B′f = Bf - 2ey (Eqn. 6-6)

ey = MZ ÷ P

ey = 620 kN-m ÷ 8070 kN = 0.077 m

B′f = 4.9 m - 2(0.077 m) = 4.75 m

L′f = Lf - 2ez (Eqn. 6-7)

ez = MY ÷ P

ez = 944.5 kN-m ÷ 8070 k (as printed, for kN) = 0.117 m

L′f = 4.9 m - 2(0.117 m) = 4.67 m

A′ = B′f · L′f = (4.75 m)(4.67 m) = 22.2 m²

Check allowable bearing stress for effective footing area:

qapplied = P ÷ A′ = 8070 kN ÷ 22.2 m² = 364 kPa

This is less than qall = 380 kPa for footings less than 5.0 m wide, according to Table B1-4, in order to limit settlement to less than 38 mm.

The design is acceptable for bearing capacity and settlement considerations.

sections.title: Example 1, Step 11 – Check overturning (eccentricity) and sliding
sections.body:
[p. B-15] Overturning will be acceptable if eccentricity in any direction is less than one-sixth the footing dimension in that direction.

(1/6)Bf = (1/6)Lf = (1/6)(4.9 m) = 0.82 m > ez > ey = 0.077 (OK)

A minimum factor of safety of 1.5 should be provided against sliding:

FS = FR / Fsliding = 0.7(W + PV) / V (FR from Step 8)

FS = 0.7(W + PV) / V

Calculate the weight of cover over the footing and the weight of footing:

The footing is bearing 2.3 m below grade. The footing can be assumed to be 0.9 m thick. [p. B-16] The area of the column is:

Acol = (π/4)(0.6 m)² = 0.28 m²

The weight of the footing and the soil cover is then (assume unit weight of concrete, γconc, of 23.5 kN/m³):

Wftg = (0.9 m)(4.9 m)(4.9 m)(23.5 kN/m³) = 508 kN

Wcover = [(1.4 m)(4.9 m)(4.9 m) - Acol(1.4 m)](19.6 kN/m³) = 651 kN

W = Wftg + Wcover = 508 kN + 651 kN = 1159 kN

So:

FS = 0.7(1159 kN + 8070 kN) / 209 kN = 31 > 1.5 (OK)

sections.title: Example 2, Step 5 – Determine the loads applied to the footing
sections.body:
[p. B-19] The superstructure loads are transmitted to the abutment at the girder-stem connection as shown in Figure B2-2. The sense of the shear force is positive if it is in the direction from the toe to the heel (right to left) and negative if opposite. The sense of the moment of the couple is positive for resisting moments (counterclockwise) and negative for overturning moments (clockwise). Moments of these loads are taken about the toe of the footing. Their sense is determined in the same manner as for the couple Mg. Application of the superstructure loads is assumed at the top of the effective abutment stem, or one-half the girder height.

Loads from the superstructure (per m length of abutment wall):

The structural engineer has determined the following.

[Table B2-1]

Dead loads of the footing and earth fill (per m length of abutment wall):

Weight of the stem, Wstem:

Wstem = γconc Tstem (Habut - Tf - 0.5Tg) = (23.5 kN/m³)(0.51 m)(5.24 m - 0.460 - 0.5(2.0 m)) = 45.30 kN/m

armstem = Dtoe + Tstem/2 = 1.22 m + 0.51 m/2 = 1.48 m

[p. B-20] Mtoe = Wstem (armstem) = (45.30 kN/m)(1.48 m) = 67.04 kN·m/m

Weight of the footing, Wf (Bf in m):

Wf = γconc Tf Bf = (23.5 kN/m³)(0.46 m)Bf = 10.81Bf kN/m

armf = Bf/2 m

Mtoe = Wf (armf) = 5.41Bf² kN·m/m

Weight of the soil over the toe, Wtoe:

Assume granular backfill for toe and heel (γ = 19.6 kN/m³, φ′ = 36°). Calculate the weight of the soil over the toe for the minimum cover.

Wtoe = γsoil (Dtoe)(Df - Tf) = (19.6 kN/m³)(1.22 m)(0.91 m) = 21.76 kN/m

armtoe = Dtoe/2 = 1.22 m/2 = 0.61 m

Mtoe = Wtoe (armtoe) = (21.76 kN/m)(0.61 m) = 13.27 kN·m/m

Weight of the soil over the heel, Wh: Bf in m

Wh = γsoil (Bf - Dtoe - Tstem)(Habut - Tf) = (19.6 kN/m³)(Bf - 1.22 m - 0.51 m)(5.24 m - 0.46 m) = (93.69)(Bf - 1.73) kN/m

[p. B-21] armh = Dtoe + Tstem + (Bf - Dtoe - Tstem)/2 = 1.22 m + 0.51 m + (Bf - 1.22 m - 0.51 m)/2 = 0.865 + 0.5Bf m

Mtoe = Wh (armh) = (93.69)(Bf - 1.73)(0.865 + 0.5Bf) kN·m/m

Loads from the approach fill:

Earth Pressure Load: It is assumed that at-rest earth pressures will exist behind the wall because the wall is restrained from rotating sufficiently to prevent active earth pressures from developing.

Assume granular backfill (γ = 19.6 kN/m³, φ′ = 36°) behind the wall. The coefficient of earth pressure at rest is

Ko = 1 - sin φ' = 1 - sin 36° = 0.41

Po = -(0.5)Ko γ Habut² = -(0.5)(0.41)(19.6 kN/m³)(5.24 m)² = -110.32 kN/m

armPo = Habut/3 = 5.24 m/3 = 1.75 m

Mtoe = Po (armPo) = (-110.32 kN/m)(1.75 m) = -193.06 kN·m/m

PLS = -(Ko γ HLS)Habut = -(0.41)(19.6 kN/m³)(0.60 m)(5.24 m) = -25.27 kN/m

[p. B-22] armLS = (0.5)Habut = (0.5)(5.24 m) = 2.62 m

Mtoe = PLS (armLS) = (-25.27 kN/m)(2.62 m) = -66.21 kN·m/m

sections.title: Example 2, Step 6 – Field exploration and laboratory testing
sections.body:
[p. B-22] This step is complete, and the subsurface data are shown in Figure B2-1. It was conservatively assumed that N′ (SPT blowcount corrected for overburden pressure) would not change after the construction of the approach embankment. For this example, the subsurface data includes the structural fill under the footing.

The initial vertical stresses are calculated using the layers shown in Figure B2-3. The initial effective vertical stresses are defined as the stresses that exist after the approach embankment is constructed up to the bearing elevation (bottom of the footing). Thus the initial vertical stresses at the midpoint of each layer are calculated as follows. It is assumed that the approach embankment is constructed to its full height concurrently with the abutment and superstructure construction.

[p. B-23] Compute the initial vertical effective stresses at the midpoints of each layer below the footing:

Layer 1: Structural fill (H1 = 2.0 m)

σ′vo1 = γ1 (H1/2) = (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m/2) = 20.5 kPa

Layer 2: Structural fill (H2 = 2.57 m)

σ′vo2 = γ1 (H1) + γ2 (H2/2) = (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.57 m/2) = 67.3 kPa

Layer 3: Well-graded clean sand (H3 = 3.0 m)

σ′vo3 = γ1 (H1) + γ2 (H2) + γ3 (H3/2) = (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.57 m) + (18.6 kN/m³)(3.0 m/2) = 121.6 kPa

[p. B-24] Layer 4: Saturated, well-graded clean sand (H4 = 3.0 m)

σ′vo4 = γ1 (H1) + γ2 (H2) + γ3 (H3) + γ′4 (H4/2) = (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.57 m) + (18.6 kN/m³)(3.0 m) + (19.6 kN/m³ - 9.81 kN/m³)(3.0 m/2) = 164.1 kPa (as printed; the terms sum to 164.2 kPa)

sections.title: Example 2, Step 7 – Calculate allowable bearing capacity
sections.body:
[p. B-24] Calculate the allowable bearing capacity, considering both the bearing capacity failure and settlement.

Calculate qall Based on Bearing Capacity Failure:

Use Equation 5-14.

qult = cNcscbc + qNqCWqsqbqdq + 0.5γBfNγCWγsγbγ (Eqn. 5-14)

In our example, the soils are all cohesionless, and c = 0. So the first term becomes zero. Assume no cover on the footing, so the second term also becomes zero. Replace Nγ with Nγq from Figure 5-7 to account for slope effects.

Look at footing widths of Bf = 2, 3, and 4 m.

Bf = 2 m:

Lf/Bf = 25.0 m / 2.0 m = 12.5 > 5

This is greater than five, so the shape factor is

sγ = 1 (Table 5-2)

The base of the footing is horizontal, so the base factor is

bγ = 1 (Table 5-5)

The water table is 4.57 m + 3.0 m = 7.57 m below the base of the footing and is greater than 1.5 Bf = (1.5)(2.0 m) = 3.0 m. Therefore the ground water correction factor is

CWγ = 1

A slope inclination angle of i = 26.6° (for 2H : 1V slope) will be used to obtain the bearing capacity factor, Nγq. Although the upper portion of the slope is flatter, this will be more conservative.

Df / Bf = 1.37 m / 2.0 m = 0.69

[p. B-25] The drained friction angle of the structural fill is assumed to be φ′ = 38°. Using Figure 5-7c, for i = 26.6° and φ′ = 38°, the following are obtained:

For Df / Bf = 0, Nγq ≅ 17.

For Df / Bf = 1, Nγq ≅ 80.

By interpolation, for Df / Bf = 0.69,

Nγq = 17 + (0.69)(80 - 17) ≅ 60

Thus

qult = 0.5γBfNγqCWγsγbγ = (0.5)(20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m)(60)(1)(1)(1) = 1230 kPa

Using a factor of safety of 3, the allowable bearing capacity is

qall = qult/3 = 1230 kPa/3 = 410 kPa

Bf = 3 m:

Proceeding in a similar manner, we obtain the following.

Lf/Bf = 25.0 m / 3.0 m = 8.33 > 5

sγ = 1, bγ = 1, and CWγ = 1.

Df / Bf = 1.37 m / 3 m = 0.46

By interpolation, for Df / Bf = 0.46,

Nγq = 17 + (0.46)(80 - 17) ≅ 46

Thus

qult = 0.5γBfNγqCWγsγbγ = (0.5)(20.5 kN/m³)(3.0 m)(46)(1)(1)(1) = 1414 kPa

[p. B-26] Using a factor of safety of 3, the allowable bearing capacity is

qall = qult/3 = 1414 kPa/3 = 471 kPa

Bf = 4 m:

Proceeding in a similar manner, we obtain the following.

Lf/Bf = 25.0 m / 4.0 m = 6.25 > 5

sγ = 1, bγ = 1, and CWγ = 1.

Df / Bf = 1.37 m / 4 m = 0.34

When Bf = 4 m, the potential failure surface can extend into Layer 3 (well-graded sand). Check to determine if the design friction angle needs to be modified for the purpose of calculating bearing capacity. From Figure B2-3, the average uncorrected SPT N-value for Layer 3 is about 24. The effective vertical stress at the midpoint of Layer 3 at the time of drilling was:

σ′vo,drilling = γ3 (H3/2) = (18.6 kN/m³)(3 m/2) = 27.9 kPa (≅ 0.58 kips/ft²)

Entering Figure 4-1 with a blowcount of 24 and a vertical effective stress of 0.58 ksf, a relative density, DR, of about 95 percent is read. Entering Figure 4-2 with this relative density for a well graded sand (Unified Soil Classification ‘SW’), a friction angle of 39 degrees is obtained. It is therefore conservative and acceptable to use φ′ of 38° to obtain Nγq.

By interpolation, for Df / Bf = 0.34,

Nγq = 17 + (0.34)(80 - 17) ≅ 38

Also use a weighted average of the soil unit weights in Layers 2 and 3:

γave = (20.5 kN/m³ + 18.6 kN/m³)/2 = 19.6 kN/m³

The bearing capacity is therefore:

qult = 0.5γave BfNγqCWγsγbγ = (0.5)(19.6 kN/m³)(4.0 m)(38)(1)(1)(1) = 1490 kPa

[p. B-27] Using a factor of safety of 3, the allowable bearing capacity is

qall = qult/3 = 1490 kPa/3 = 497 kPa

Calculate qall based on allowable settlement:

To estimate the bridge loading to generate 25 mm of settlement, use both the Hough method and D’Appolonia’s method. Use the Hough method to estimate the settlement in the structural fill Layers 1 and 2. However, because the native sand of Layers 3 and 4 is known to be geologically preloaded, use D’Appolonia’s method to avoid overestimating the settlement in these layers. The total settlement can be calculated by summing the settlements in each layer.

The Hough method estimates settlements based on average changes in stress for the layer. D’Appolonia’s method estimates settlements based on the applied stress at the top of the layer. Therefore, calculate the stress increase at the midpoint of Layers 1 and 2, and at the top of Layer 3 using the 2-on-1 stress distribution method for footing widths of Bf = 2, 3, 4 m.

Δσv/q = BfLf / ((Bf + Z)(Lf + Z)) (Eqn. 5-17)

where q = bridge loading per unit area at the base of the footing

Z = depth to the midpoint of a layer

Using this equation, Δσv/q, the stress increases due to bridge footing loads are summarized in Table B2-3.

[Table B2-3]

Use the Hough method to estimate the settlement in Layers 1 and 2. The general equation is:

ΔH = Ho (1/C′) log((σ′vo + Δσvf) / σ′vo) (Eqn. 5-24)

Bearing capacity index (C′) for the structural fill of layers 1 and 2 is obtained from Figure 5-19. For structural fill consisting of well-graded silty sand & gravel, use the recommended corrected [p. B-28] SPT N-value for compacted structural fill of 32. Entering Figure 5-19 with N′ = 32 for well-graded silty sand and gravel, a C′ of 110 is read.

For a footing pressure, q, of 100 kPa and a footing width of Bf = 2 m, the settlement in Layers 1 and 2 are calculated as follows.

Layer 1:

ΔH1 = H1 (1/C1') log((σ′vo1 + (Δσv1/q)(q)) / σ′vo1) = (2 m)(1/110) log((20.5 kPa + (0.64)(100 kPa)) / 20.5 kPa) = 0.0112 m = 11.2 mm

Layer 2:

ΔH2 = H2 (1/C2') log((σ′vo2 + (Δσv2/q)(q)) / σ′vo2) = (2.57 m)(1/110) log((67.3 kPa + (0.33)(100 kPa)) / 67.3 kPa) = 0.004 m = 4 mm

Use D’Appolonia’s method to estimate the settlement in Layers 3 and 4. General equation is:

ΔH = (ΔσV Bf / M) μo μ1 (Eqn. 5-25)

The modulus of compressibility of sand and gravel (M) for Layers 3 and 4 is obtained from Figure 5-21, and the correction factors (μo and μ1) are obtained from Figure 5-20. Combining Layers 3 and 4 into one layer, the average uncorrected SPT N-value for the layer is 30. Entering Figure 5-21 with an average uncorrected blowcount of 30 and an M of 750 tsf, or 71820 kPa, is read for preloaded sand. Entering the upper chart of Figure 5-20 for D = 4.57 m and B = 6.57 to 8.57 m (based on the 2-on-1 stress distribution method and Bf = 2, 3, and 4 m), a μo of 0.74 is read. Entering the lower chart of Figure 5-20 for H = 6 m and B = 6.57 to 8.57 m, a μ1 of 0.25 is read.

[p. B-29] For a footing pressure of 100 kPa and a footing width of Bf = 2 m, the settlement in layers 3 and 4 are calculated as follows.

ΔH3,4 = ((Δσv3,4/q)(q)(Bf) / M3,4) μo μ1 = (0.26(100 kPa)(6.57 m) / 71820 kPa)(0.74)(0.25) = 0.0004 m = 0.4 mm (as printed; the formula names Bf, 2 m here, but the line puts in 6.57 m, the B with which p. B-28 enters Figure 5-20 for Bf = 2 m; with 2 m the line gives 0.0001 m)

The total settlement is therefore:

ΣΔHi = 11.2 + 4.0 + 0.4 = 16 mm

In a similar manner, the settlements for different widths and bridge loadings are obtained and are summarized as follows.

[Table B2-4]

Table B2-4 shows that the maximum allowable footing pressure to limit the settlement to 25 mm decreases from about 233 kPa for Bf = 2 m to about 163 kPa for Bf = 4 m. These values are smaller than the qall values based on bearing capacity failure that were calculated earlier.

Settlement will therefore limit the allowable bearing capacity for the design of this footing. Interpolating the values in Table B2-4, find ranges of footing widths that will limit settlement to 25 mm or less at nominal allowable bearing capacities of 150 kPa, 190 kPa and 230 kPa. These are summarized in Table B2-5.

[p. B-30] [Table B2-5]

The geotechnical engineer should provide this table to the structural designer for sizing of the footing.

sections.title: Example 2, Step 8 – Calculate sliding and passive soil resistance
sections.body:
[p. B-30] The footing concrete will be poured on compacted structural fill. Therefore, the friction angle, δ, to be used in the sliding analysis of the footing will be δ = φ′ = 38°.

The passive resistance of the soil in front of the footing will be ignored. The ultimate sliding resistance is therefore:

FR = (W + Pv) tan δ (Eqn. 5-38) = (W + Pv) tan(38°) = 0.78(W + Pv)

sections.body: [p. B-30] The geotechnical engineer has checked an abutment and approach embankment with the same dimensions and similar loading conditions but with a weaker foundation soil (silt with N′ = 10) and found that the minimum factor of safety was about 1.6 and satisfactory (see Example 3). Thus, with stronger foundation soils, the factor of safety should be greater than 1.6 and satisfactory.

sections.title: Example 2, Step 10 – Size the footing under full loading
sections.body:
[p. B-30] From Table B2-1, the total vertical load from the superstructure is

Pv structure = DC + DW + LL + BR = 169.22 kN/m + 19.99 kN/m + 48.60 kN/m + 0.58 kN/m = 238.39 kN/m

Referring to Table B2-2, the additional load from the abutment components per 1-m length of the abutment wall for Bf = 3 m is

[p. B-31] Wstem = 45.30 kN/m

Wf = 10.81Bf = (10.81)(3) = 32.43 kN/m

Wtoe = 21.76 kN/m

Wh = (93.69)(Bf - 1.73) = (93.69)(3 - 1.73) = 118.99 kN/m

Pv abut = 45.30 + 32.43 + 21.76 + 118.99 = 218.48 kN/m

Thus

Pv = Pv structure + Pv abut = 238.39 kN/m + 218.48 kN/m = 457 kN/m

From Table B2-5, an allowable bearing pressure of 190 kPa may be applied by the footing if Bf = 2 to 3 m. Using a footing pressure of 190 kPa, the required footing width Bf is

Bf = Pv/(190 kPa) = (457 kN/m)/(190 kPa) = 2.40 m

This satisfies Bf = 2 to 3 m but appears to be too small to meet overturning requirements for Habut = 5.24 m. A preliminary dimension for a footing width can be estimated as one-half the abutment height, or Habut = (0.5)(5.24 m) = 2.62 m (as printed; the value is the footing width, one-half of Habut = 5.24 m, so the left side is Bf). Therefore, try Bf = 2.7 m.

sections.title: Example 2, Step 11 – Check overturning and sliding under full loading
sections.body:
[p. B-31] Check overturning for Bf = 2.7 m:

Analyze for 1 m of abutment wall length.

From Step 10 and Table B2-1, the loads and moments due to the superstructure are

Pv structure = 238.39 kN/m

Mtoe structure = 272.27 kN·m/m + 42.61 kN·m/m + 103.17 kN·m/m + 6.31 kN·m/m = 424.36 kN·m/m

Referring to Table B2-2, the loads and moments due to abutment components are

Pv abut = 45.30 + 10.81Bf + 21.76 + (93.69)(Bf - 1.73) = 45.30 + (10.81)(2.7) + 21.76 + (93.69)(2.7 - 1.73) = 187.13 kN/m

[p. B-32] Mtoe abut = 67.04 + 5.41Bf² + 13.27 + (93.69)(Bf - 1.73)(0.865 + 0.5Bf) - 193.06 - 66.21 = 67.04 + (5.41)(2.7)² + 13.27 + (93.69)(2.7 - 1.73)(0.865 + (0.5)(2.7)) - 193.06 - 66.21 = 61.78 kN·m/m

The total loads and moments are:

Pv = Pv structure + Pv abut = 238.39 kN/m + 187.13 kN/m = 425.52 kN/m

Mtoe = Mtoe structure + Mtoe abut = 424.36 kN·m/m + 61.78 kN·m/m = 486.14 kN·m/m

The arm of the resultant is

armR = Mtoe/Pv = (486.14 kN·m/m)/(425.52 kN/m) = 1.14 m

The eccentricity, ey, is

ey = Bf/2 - armR = 2.7 m/2 - 1.14 m = 1.35 m - 1.14 m = 0.21 m

For stability, the eccentricity should be less than one-sixth the footing width:

ey = 0.21 m < Bf/6 = 2.7 m/6 = 0.45 m (OK)

Check bearing stress for effective footing area:

B′f = Bf - 2ey = 2.7 m - (2)(0.21 m) = 2.28 m

[p. B-33] qfooting = Pv/B′f = (425.52 kN/m)(2.28 m) (as printed; the value is 425.52 kN/m divided by 2.28 m) = 186.6 kPa

From Table B2-5, the allowable bearing pressure for B′f = 2 to 3 m is 190 kPa. Therefore, qfooting < qall and the bearing stress is smaller than the allowable value. (OK)

Check sliding:

In Table B2-1, the vehicular live load (LL) and the vehicular braking force (BR) act to resist sliding. To be conservative, these two loads will be ignored in the sliding analysis. The forces that tend to induce sliding are the sum of the following:

Shear from the dead load of components, DC (Table B2-1)

Shear from the dead load of wearing surfaces, DW (Table B2-1)

At-rest earth pressure load, Po (Table B2-2)

Horizontal earth load from live load surcharge, PLS (Table B2-2)

Analyzing per m length of the abutment wall, Fsliding is

Fsliding = DC + DW + Po + PLS = 42.61 + 16.64 - 110.32 - 25.27 = -76.34 kN/m

The force FR available to resist sliding (from Step 8) is

FR = 0.78(W + Pv)

Neglecting the vehicular live load (LL) and vehicular breaking force (BR):

Pv structure = DC + DW = 169.22 + 19.99 kN/m = 189.21 kN/m

W = Pv abut = 187.13 kN/m

[p. B-34] The factor of safety FS against sliding is

FS = FR/Fsliding = 0.78(189.21 kN/m + 187.13 kN/m) / 76.34 kN/m = 293.54 kN/m (as printed; 0.78 × 376.34 = 293.55) / 76.34 kN/m = 3.8

FS > 1.5 (OK)

sections.body:
[p. B-35] Given:

• A seat-type abutment on a spread footing is proposed for a bridge.

• There is no scour potential at this site.

• The footing length is L = 25.0 m (82 ft); other dimensions are shown in Figure B3-1.

• The approach embankment and the foundation conditions are shown in Figure B3-1.

• The SPT hammer energy ratio is assumed to be ER = 60%.

• Frost penetration depth is 0.6 m (2 ft).

• Tolerable settlement is 38 mm (1.5 in).

• Abutment loading symbols are shown in Figure B3-2.

Find:

• Size the footing based on Service Load Design, Group IV loads (allowable stress design method), considering both settlement and bearing capacity. Check overturning and sliding.

[p. B-37] Solution:

Steps 1 through 4 – Preliminary bridge layout, review of existing geologic and subsurface data, site reconnaissance, scour and frost potential:

The structural, hydraulic and geotechnical engineers completed these steps. The required design information is provided in the problem-given statement.

Given, Find, and Steps 1 through 4 (preliminary layout, existing data, reconnaissance, scour and frost); the calculation steps follow as their own sections.

sections.title: Example 3, Step 5 – Determine the loads applied to the footing
sections.body:
[p. B-37] Moments are taken about the front toe of the footing. The direction of the moment is positive for resisting moments (counterclockwise) and negative for overturning moments (clockwise).

Loads from the girders:

The structural engineer has provided Group IV loads as summarized in Table B3-1. Recall that Group IV is the SLD load combination with normal vehicles using the bridge without wind, and with consideration of long term shrinkage, shortening, and thermal movements.

[Table B3-1]

Dead loads of the abutment components (per m of abutment wall, assume γconcrete = 23.5 kN/m³)

Weight of the stem, Wstem (for simplicity, this computation does not subtract out the weight of the seat):

Wstem = γconc Tstem (Habut - Tf) = (23.5 kN/m³)(0.51 m)(5.24 m - 0.46 m) = 57.29 kN/m

armstem = Dtoe + Tstem/2 = 1.22 m + 0.51 m/2 = 1.48 m

[p. B-38] Mtoe = Wstem (armstem) = (57.29 kN/m)(1.48 m) = 84.79 kN·m/m

Weight of the footing, Wf (Bf in m):

Wf = γconc Tf Bf = (23.5 kN/m³)(0.46 m)Bf = 10.81Bf kN/m

armf = Bf/2 m

Mtoe = Wf (armf) = 5.41Bf² kN·m/m

In this example, the weight of the soil over the toe, Wtoe, is ignored for design purposes because the soil may not get placed until after the bridge superstructure is constructed. Assume granular backfill for toe and heel (γ = 19.6 kN/m³, φ′ = 36°).

Weight of the soil over the heel, Wh (Bf in m):

Wh = γsoil (Bf - Dtoe - Tstem)(Habut - Tf) = (19.6 kN/m³)(Bf - 1.22 m - 0.51 m)(5.24 m - 0.46 m) = (93.69)(Bf - 1.73) kN/m

armh = Dtoe + Tstem + (Bf - Dtoe - Tstem)/2 = 1.22 m + 0.51 m + (Bf - 1.22 m - 0.51 m)/2 = 0.865 + 0.5Bf m

Mtoe = Wh (armh) = (93.69)(Bf - 1.73)(0.865 + 0.5Bf) kN·m/m

Loads from Approach Fill:

Active earth pressure: Assume that the stem wall will rotate sufficiently to develop active earth pressures behind the wall. Use Rankine’s active earth pressure coefficient. Assume granular backfill (γ = 19.6 kN/m³, φ′ = 36°) behind the wall.

[p. B-39] Ka = tan²(45° - φ'/2) (Eqn. 6-3) = tan²(45° - 36°/2) = 0.26

PA = (0.5)Ka γ Habut² = (0.5)(0.26)(19.6 kN/m³)(5.24)² = 69.96 kN/m

armPA = Habut/3 = 5.24 m/3 = 1.75 m

Mtoe = -PA (armPA) = -(69.96 kN/m)(1.75 m) = -122.43 kN·m/m

Horizontal earth pressure from live load surcharge (use HLS = 0.60 m):

PLS = (Ka γ HLS)Habut = (0.26)(19.6 kN/m³)(0.60 m)(5.24 m) = 16.02 kN/m

armLS = (0.5)Habut = (0.5)(5.24 m) = 2.62 m

Mtoe = -PLS (armLS) = -(16.02 kN/m)(2.62 m) = -41.97 kN·m/m

These loads are summarized in Table B3-2.

sections.title: Example 3, Step 6 – Conduct subsurface exploration and laboratory testing
sections.body:
[p. B-40] This step is complete, and the subsurface data are shown in Figure B3-1. It was conservatively assumed that N′ (SPT blowcount corrected for overburden pressure) would not change after the construction of the approach embankment. For this example, the subsurface data include the structural fill under the footing.

The initial vertical stresses are calculated using the layers shown in Figure B3-3. The initial vertical stresses were calculated as the stresses that exist after the approach embankment is constructed to its full height. These are estimated by using the depth from the estimated ground surface of the approach embankment after its construction, as shown in Figure B3-3. The initial vertical stresses at the midpoint of each layer are calculated as follows.

Layer 1: Structural fill (H1 = 2.0 m); note that the height of backfill is taken as the average height of the surcharge at the stem:

σ′vo1 = γbackfill (3.5 m) + γ1 (H1/2) = (19.6 kN/m³)(3.5 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m/2) = 89.1 kPa

Layer 2: Structural fill (H2 = 2.57 m)

σ′vo2 = γbackfill (3.5 m) + γ1H1 + γ2 (H2/2) = (19.6 kN/m³)(3.5 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.57 m/2) = 135.9 kPa

[p. B-41] Layer 3: Silt (H3 = 3.0 m)

σ′vo3 = γbackfill (3.5 m) + γ1H1 + γ2H2 + γ3 (H3/2) = (19.6 kN/m³)(3.5 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.57 m) + (17.3 kN/m³)(3.0 m/2) = 188.2 kPa

[p. B-42] Layer 4: Silt (H4 = 3.0 m)

σ′vo4 = γbackfill (3.5 m) + γ1H1 + γ2H2 + γ3 (H3) + γ4 (H4/2) = (19.6 kN/m³)(3.5 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.57 m) + (17.3 kN/m³)(3.0 m) + (17.3 kN/m³)(3.0 m/2) = 240.1 kPa

Layer 5: Saturated silty sand (H5 = 3.0 m)

σ′vo5 = γbackfill (3.5 m) + γ1H1 + γ2H2 + γ3 (H3) + γ4 (H4) + γ5 (H5/2) = (19.6 kN/m³)(3.5 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.57 m) + (17.3 kN/m³)(3.0 m) + (17.3 kN/m³)(3.0 m) + (19.6 - 9.81 kN/m³)(3.0 m/2) = 280.7 kPa (as printed; the terms sum to 280.8 kPa)

Layer 6: Saturated silty sand (H6 = 3.0 m)

σ′vo6 = γbackfill (3.5 m) + γ1H1 + γ2H2 + γ3 (H3) + γ4 (H4) + γ5 (H5) + γ6 (H6/2) = (19.6 kN/m³)(3.5 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.0 m) + (20.5 kN/m³)(2.57 m) + (17.3 kN/m³)(3.0 m) + (17.3 kN/m³)(3.0 m) + (19.6 - 9.81 kN/m³)(3.0 m) + (19.6 - 9.81 kN/m³)(3.0 m/2) = 310.1 kPa

sections.title: Example 3, Step 7 – Calculate allowable bearing capacity
sections.body:
[p. B-42] Calculate the allowable bearing capacity, considering both bearing capacity failure and settlement.

First calculate qall using bearing capacity theory:

qult = cNcscbc + qNqCWqsqbqdq + 0.5γBfNγCWγsγbγ (Eqn. 5-14)

In this example, the soils are all cohesionless, and c = 0. So the first term becomes zero. Assume no cover on the footing, so the second term also becomes zero. Replace Nγ with Nγq from Figure 5-7 to account for slope effects.

Look at footing widths of Bf = 3, 4 and 5 m.

[p. B-43] Bf = 3 m:

Lf/Bf = 25.0 m / 3.0 m = 8.33 > 5

This ratio is greater than five, so the shape factor is

sγ = 1 (Table 5-2)

The base of the footing is horizontal, therefore the base factor is

bγ = 1 (Table 5-5)

The water table is 4.57 m + 6.0 m = 10.57 m below the base of the footing and is greater than 1.5 Bf = (1.5)(3.0 m) = 4.5 m. Therefore, the ground water correction factor is

CWγ = 1 (Table 5-3)

A slope inclination angle of i = 26.6° (for 2H : 1V slope) will be used to obtain the bearing capacity factor Nγq. This will be conservative, even though the upper portion of the slope is flatter.

Df / Bf = 1.37 m / 3.0 m = 0.46

The drained friction angle of the structural fill is assumed to be φ′ = 38°. Using Figure 5-7f, for i = 26.6° and φ′ = 38°, the following are obtained (as printed; Figure 5-7f, p. 59, is entered with the distance of the foundation from the edge of the slope, b/Bf, which this step does not give; Example 2, p. B-25, reads the same 17 and 80 for the same i and φ′ from Figure 5-7c, the chart entered with the inclination of the slope):

For Df / Bf = 0, Nγq ≅ 17.

For Df / Bf = 1, Nγq ≅ 80.

By interpolation, for Df / Bf = 0.46,

Nγq = 17 + (0.46)(80 - 17) ≅ 46

The ultimate bearing capacity is

qult = 0.5γBfNγqCWγsγbγ = (0.5)(20.5 kN/m³)(3.0 m)(46)(1)(1)(1) = 1414 kPa

[p. B-44] Using a factor of safety of 3, the allowable bearing capacity is

qall = qult/3 = 1414 kPa/3 = 471 kPa

Bf = 4 m:

Proceeding in a similar manner,

Lf/Bf = 25.0 m / 4.0 m = 6.25 > 5

sγ = 1, bγ = 1, and CWγ = 1

Df / Bf = 1.37 m / 4 m = 0.34

By interpolation, for Df / Bf = 0.34,

When Bf = 4 m, the potential failure surface can extend into Unit 3 (silt). To determine how much of the failure surface will engage Unit 3, use the rule of thumb that the failure surface will extend to a maximum depth of about 1.5 times the footing width, or in this case 1.5(4 m) = 6 m. This extends about 1.5 m into Unit 3, which corresponds to about one-half of the failure surface passing through Unit 3 (visually estimated from Figure B3-1). Therefore, use a weighted average friction angle to obtain Nγq. A design friction angle associated with Layer 3 is needed.

From Figure B3-3, the average uncorrected SPT N-value for this layer is about 5.2. The effective vertical stress at the midpoint at the time of drilling was:

σ′v drilling = γ3 (H3/2) = (17.3 kN/m³)(3 m/2) = 25.95 kPa ≅ 0.54 kips/ft²

Entering Figure 4-1 with a blowcount of 5.2 and a vertical effective stress of 0.54 ksf, a relative density, DR, of about 50 percent is read. Entering Figure 4-2 with this relative density for lean silt (Unified Soil Classification ‘ML’), a friction angle of 32° is obtained. Use a reduced φ′ from 38° to 34° to obtain Nγq. Using Figure 5-7, for i = 26.6° and φ′ = 34°, the following is obtained:

Nγq = 12 + (0.34)(43 - 12) ≅ 23

Use a weighted average of the soil unit weights in Units 2 and 3:

γaverage = (20.5 kN/m³ + 17.3 kN/m (as printed, for kN/m³))/2 = 18.9 kN/m³

[p. B-45] The ultimate bearing capacity is

qult = 0.5γBfNγqCWγsγbγ = (0.5)(18.9 kN/m³)(4.0 m)(23)(1)(1)(1) = 869 kPa

Using a factor of safety of 3, the allowable bearing capacity is

qall = qult/3 = 869 kPa/3 = 290 kPa

Bf = 5 m:

Proceeding in a similar manner,

Lf/Bf = 25.0 m / 5.0 m = 5

sγ = 1, bγ = 1, and CWγ = 1.

Df / Bf = 1.37 m / 5 m = 0.27

When Bf = 5 m, the potential failure surface can extend deeply into Unit 3 (silt). Therefore, conservatively use Unit 3 soil properties (γ = 17.3 kN/m³, φ = 32 degrees) to compute bearing capacity:

For Df / Bf = 0, Nγq ≅ 7.

For Df / Bf = 1, Nγq ≅ 32.

By interpolation, for Df / Bf = 0.27,

Nγq = 7 + (0.27)(32 - 7) ≅ 14

Thus

qult = 0.5γBfNγqCWγsγbγ = (0.5)(17.3 kN/m³)(5.0 m)(14)(1)(1)(1) = 605 kPa

[p. B-46] Using a factor of safety of 3, the allowable bearing capacity is

qall = qult/3 = 605 kPa/3 = 202 kPa

Calculate qall based on allowable settlement:

Since the embankment weight is so large, settlement due to approach embankment construction is, in general, much greater than the settlement due to bridge loading alone. Due to the presence of the compressible silt, the settlement due to the approach embankment alone was computed using the FHWA program EMBANK. The input parameters for soil unit weight and compression index shown below were estimated from the subsurface exploration SPT N-values per the Hough method. The EMBANK output is shown in Figure B3-4.

[p. B-47] The settlement was computed to be 186 mm. This is excessive for the bridge. It will therefore be necessary to mitigate the settlement by surcharging the site prior to construction of the abutment foundation. The contract will specify that the embankment must be built full height and to full dimensions and settlement monitored until complete, before excavating back down to the bearing elevation and constructing the footing. Since the settlement potential is mostly due to the inelastic silt layer, the settlement should occur relatively quickly, and the potential for post-construction settlement due to secondary consolidation (creep) will be low. Therefore, a spread footing is still a cost-effective foundation choice for this site.

The design of the abutment footing will therefore need to consider only the potential settlement due to the structure loads, as follows:

Calculate the stress increase at the midpoint of each soil layer using the 2-on-1 stress distribution method for footing widths of Bf = 3, 4, 5 m.

Δσv/q = BfLf / ((Bf + Z)(Lf + Z)) (Eqn. 5-17)

Using this equation, Δσv/q ratios are tabulated in Table B3-3.

[Table B3-3]

Use the Hough method to estimate the bridge loading to generate 38 mm of settlement.

General equation is:

ΔH = Ho (1/C′) log((σ'vo + Δσv) / σ′vo) (Eqn. 5-24)

Bearing capacity index (C′) of the layers are obtained from Figure 5-19 as follows. This assumes N, and therefore N′ is unchanged after pre-loading, which is conservative.

Layers 1 and 2: Structural fill consisting of well-graded silty sand & gravel [p. B-48] Use the recommended assumed corrected SPT N-value for compacted structural fill:

N' = 32

From Figure 5-19, C′1,2 = 110.

Layer 3: Alluvium consisting of inorganic silt

Nave = 5.2 (Figure B3-3)

The effective vertical pressure at the time of drilling was

σ′vo drilling3 = γ3 (H3/2) = (17.3 kN/m³)(3 m/2) = 25.9 kPa

Thus N′/N = 1.92 (Figure 5-18).

N′ = 10

C′3 = 30 (Figure 5-19)

Layer 4: Alluvium consisting of inorganic silt

Nave = 9.0 (Figure B3-3)

σ′vo drilling4 = σ′vo drilling3 + γ3 (H3/2) + γ4 (H4/2) = 25.95 kPa + (17.3 kN/m³)(3 m/2) + (17.3 kN/m³)(3 m/2) = 25.95 kPa + 25.95 kPa + 25.95 kPa = 77.8 kPa

N′/N = 1.11 (Figure 5-18)

N′ = 10

C′4 = 30 (Figure 5-19)

Layer 5: Alluvium consisting of well-graded fine to medium sand

Nave = 17.0 (Figure B3-3)

σ′vo drilling5 = σ′vo drilling4 + γ4 (H4/2) + γ′5 (H5/2) = 77.85 kPa + (17.3 kN/m³)(3 m/2) + (19.6 - 9.81 kN/m³(3 m/2) = 77.85 kPa + 25.95 kPa + 14.69 kPa = 118.5 kPa

[p. B-49] N′/N = 0.9 (Figure 5-18)

N′ = 15

C′5 = 50 (Figure 5-19)

Layer 6: Alluvium consisting of well-graded fine to medium sand

Nave = 25.0 (Figure B3-3)

σ′vo drilling6 = σ′vo drilling5 + γ′5 (H5/2) + γ′6 (H6/2) = 118.49 kPa + (19.6 - 9.81 kN/m³(3 m/2) + (19.6 - 9.81 kN/m³(3 m/2) = 118.49 kPa + 14.69 kPa + 14.69 kPa = 147.9 kPa

N′/N = 0.805 (Figure 5-18)

N′ = 20

C′6 = 58 (Figure 5-19)

The total settlement can be calculated by summing the settlements in each layer. For a range of bridge loadings from, say, q = 100 kPa to 300 kPa and footing widths of Bf = 3 m to 5 m, the settlements are calculated as follows:

Layer 1:

ΔH1 = H1 (1/C′1) log((σ′vo1 + Δσv1) / σ′vo1) = 2 m (1/110) log((89.1 kPa + (0.72)(100 kPa)) / 89.1 kPa) = 0.0047 m ≅ 5 mm

Layer 2:

ΔH2 = H2 (1/C′2) log((σ′vo2 + Δσv2) / σ′vo2) = 2.57 m (1/110) log((135.9 kPa + (0.42)(100 kPa)) / 135.9 kPa) = 0.0027 m ≅ 3 mm

[p. B-50] Layer 3:

ΔH3 = H3 (1/C′3) log((σ′vo3 + Δσv3) / σ′vo3) = 3.0 m (1/30) log((188.2 kPa + (0.27)(100 kPa)) / 188.2 kPa) = 0.0058 m ≅ 6 mm

Layer 4:

ΔH4 = H4 (1/C′4) log((σ′vo4 + Δσv4) / σ′vo4) = 3.0 m (1/30) log((240.1 kPa + (0.18)(100 kPa)) / 240.1 kPa) = 0.0031 m ≅ 3 mm

Layer 5:

ΔH5 = H5 (1/C′5) log((σ′vo5 + Δσv5) / σ′vo5) = 3.0 m (1/50) log((280.7 kPa + (0.13)(100 kPa)) / 280.7 kPa) = 0.0012 m ≅ 1 mm

Layer 6:

ΔH6 = H6 (1/C′6) log((σ′vo6 + Δσv6) / σ′vo6) = 3.0 m (1/58) log((310.1 kPa + (0.10)(100 kPa)) / 310.1 kPa) = 0.0007 m ≅ 1 mm

The total settlement is:

ΣΔHi = 5 + 3 + 6 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 19 mm

In a similar manner, the settlements for different footing widths and bridge loadings are calculated and summarized in Table B3-4.

[p. B-51] [Table B3-4]

Table B3-4 shows that the maximum allowable q to limit the settlement to 38 mm decreases from about 238 kPa for Bf = 3 m to about 178 kPa for Bf = 5 m. These values are smaller than the qall values based on bearing capacity failure that were calculated earlier. Therefore, the settlement will limit the allowable bearing capacity of the footings.

The allowable bearing pressure is summarized in Figure B3-5.

sections.title: Example 3, Step 8 – Calculate sliding and passive soil resistance
sections.body:
[p. B-51] The footing concrete will be poured on compacted structural fill. Thus the friction angle, δ, to be used in the sliding analysis of the footing will be δ = φ′ = 38°.

The passive resistance of the soil in front of the footing will be ignored. The ultimate sliding resistance is therefore:

FR = (W + Pv) tan δ (Eqn. 5-38) = (W + Pv) tan(38°) = 0.78(W + Pv)

B-51).

sections.title: Example 3, Step 9 – Check global stability of the footing
sections.body: [p. B-52] The slope stability program XSTABL™ was used to evaluate the global stability of the approach embankment with the abutment and the bridge loading applied. The program uses Bishop’s method of slices to compute a global stability factor of safety for the slope. A footing width of Bf = 3.5 m was assumed. The footing loads and the abutment backfill were modeled as applied vertical surcharge loads at the footing bearing elevation. The applied footing stress corresponded to the allowable bearing pressure for this footing width (e.g., 240 kPa from Figure B3-4) (as printed; the allowable bearing pressure is plotted in Figure B3-5, which for Bf = 3.5 m reads about 219 kPa; Table B3-4, p. B-51, gives 38 mm at about 238 kPa for Bf = 3 m and at 200 kPa for 4 m, so about 219 kPa at 3.5 m, and 240 kPa is about the value for Bf = 3 m). At this stress, the critical failure surface was just behind the heel of the footing. The minimum factor of safety was about 1.6 and satisfactory. The potential failure arc is shown in Figure B3-6.

B-52).

sections.title: Example 3, Step 10 – Size the footing under full loading
sections.body:
[p. B-52] From Table B3-1, the total vertical load from the bridge girders is

P = DC + DW + LL = 5233 kN + 446 kN + 1538 kN = 7217 kN

Using Lf = 25 m,

[p. B-53] Pv girders = P / Lf = 7217 kN / 25 m = 288.7 kN/m

The additional load from the abutment components per 1-m length of the abutment wall is calculated as follows for Bf = 3 m.

Wstem = 57.29 kN/m

Wf = 10.81Bf = (10.81)(3) = 32.43 kN/m

Wh = (93.69)(Bf - 1.73) = (93.69)(3 - 1.73) = 118.99 kN/m

Pv abut = 57.29 + 32.43 + 118.99 = 208.71 kN/m

Thus

Pv = Pv girders + Pv abut = 288.7 kN/m + 208.7 kN/m ≅ 497 kN/m

From Figure B3-4 (as printed; the allowable bearing pressure is plotted in Figure B3-5), a bearing pressure of up to 230 kPa may be applied by the footing. Using q = 230 kPa, the required footing width Bf is

Bf = Pv / q = (497 kN/m)/(230 kPa) = 2.16 m

This appears to be too small for Habut = 5.24 m. A preliminary dimension for a footing width can be estimated as one-half the abutment height, or Habut = (0.5)(5.24 m) = 2.62 m (as printed; the value is the footing width, one-half of Habut = 5.24 m, so the left side is Bf). Therefore, try Bf = 2.7 m.
sections.applicability: Appendix B, Example 3 (a stub seat-type abutment footing in compacted structural fill over compressible silt, with the approach embankment settlement (EMBANK) and bearing pad shears; Service Load Design, Group IV loads), printed heading Step 10 – Size the footing under full loading (pp. B-52 to B-53).

sections.title: Example 3, Step 11a – Check overturning (eccentricity), bearing pressure and sliding under full loading without PDW and PLL
sections.body:
[p. B-53] Check overturning for Bf = 2.7 m:

Analyze for 1 m of abutment length.

From Table B3-1, the loads and moments due to girders are

[p. B-54] Pv girders = 5233 kN / Lf = 5233 kN / 25 m = 209.3 kN/m

Mtoe girders = (7274 - 3392) kN·m / Lf = 3882 kN·m / 25 m = 155.3 kN·m/m

From Table B3-2, the loads and moments due to abutment components are

Pv abut = 57.29 + 10.81Bf + (93.69)(Bf - 1.73) kN/m = 57.29 + (10.81)(2.7) + (93.69)(2.7 - 1.73) kN/m = 177.4 kN/m

Mtoe abut = 84.79 + 5.41Bf² + (93.69)(Bf - 1.73)(0.865 + 0.5Bf) - 122.43 - 41.97 = 84.79 + (5.41)(2.7)² + (93.69)(2.7 m - 1.73)(0.865 + (0.5)(2.7 m)) - 122.43 - 41.97 = 161.1 kN·m/m

The total loads are

Pv = Pv girders + Pv abut = 209.3 kN/m + 177.4 kN/m = 386.7 kN/m

Mtoe = Mtoe girders + Mtoe abut = 155.3 kN·m/m + 161.1 kN·m/m = 316.4 kN·m/m

The arm of the resultant is

armR = Mtoe / Pv = (316.4 kN·m/m)/(386.7 kN/m) = 0.82 m

[p. B-55] The eccentricity, ey, is

ey = Bf/2 - armR = 2.7 m/2 - 0.82 m = 1.35 m - 0.82 m = 0.53 m

For stability, the eccentricity should be less than one-sixth the footing width:

ey = 0.53 m < Bf/6 = 2.7 m/6 = 0.45 m (No Good) (as printed; 0.53 m is greater than 0.45 m)

Try increasing Bf to 3.2 m.

Check overturning for Bf = 3.2 m:

Analyze for 1 m of abutment length.

From the previous calculations, the loads and moments due to girders are

Pv girders = 209.3 kN/m

Mtoe girders = 155.3 kN·m/m

From Table B3-2, the loads and moments due to abutment components are

Pv abut = 57.29 + 10.81Bf + (93.69)(Bf - 1.73) kN/m = 57.29 + (10.81)(3.2) + (93.69)(3.2 - 1.73) kN/m = 229.6 kN/m

Mtoe abut = 84.79 + 5.41Bf² + (93.69)(Bf - 1.73)(0.865 + 0.5Bf) - 122.43 - 41.97 = 84.79 + (5.41)(3.2)² + (93.69)(3.2 m - 1.73)(0.865 + (0.5)(3.2 m)) - 122.43 - 41.97 = 315.3 kN·m/m

The total loads are

Pv = Pv griders + Pv abut = 209.3 kN/m + 229.6 kN/m = 438.9 kN/m

[p. B-56] Mtoe = Mtoe girders + Mtoe abut = 155.3 kN·m/m + 315.3 kN·m/m = 470.6 kN·m/m

The arm of the resultant is

armR = Mtoe / Pv = (470.6 kN·m/m)/(438.9 kN/m) = 1.07 m

The eccentricity, ey, is

ey = Bf/2 - armR = 3.2 m/2 - 1.07 m = 1.6 m - 1.07 m = 0.527 m (as printed; 1.6 m - 1.07 m = 0.53 m, and with the arm unrounded 0.528 m)

For stability, the eccentricity should be less than one-sixth the footing width:

ey = 0.527 m < Bf/6 = 3.2 m/6 = 0.533 m (OK)

Check bearing stress for effective footing area:

B′f = Bf - 2ey (Eqn. 6-6) = 3.2 m - (2)(0.53 m) = 2.14 m

q = Pv / B′f = (438.9 kN/m)/(2.14 m) = 205.1 kPa

By extrapolating the values in Figure B3-4 (as printed; the allowable bearing pressure is plotted in Figure B3-5), the allowable bearing pressure for B′f = 2.14 m to limit settlement to less than 38 mm is about

qall = 275 kPa

Under Group IV loads, the 25 percent overstress allowance can be applied to this allowable bearing pressure. By inspection, however, this computation is not necessary since q < qall, and the bearing stress is smaller than the allowable value. (OK)

Check sliding:

The forces, Fsliding, that tend to induce sliding are the sum of the following:

[p. B-57] Shear loads from bearing pads, V (Table B3-1)

Active earth pressure load, PA (Table B3-2)

Horizontal earth load from live load surcharge, PLS (Table B3-2)

Analyzing per m of the abutment wall, Fsliding is

Fsliding = V/Lf + PA + PLS = 1047 kN/25 m + 69.96 kN/m + 16.02 kN/m = 127.9 kN/m

The force, FR, available to resist sliding (from Step 8) is

FR = 0.78(W + Pv)

The vertical force, Pv computed above includes the self-weight of the footing, W. The live load and weight of the wearing surface should not be included in this calculation. Thus the factor of safety FS against sliding is

FSsliding = FR / Fsliding ≥ 1.5 (Eqn. 5-40) = 0.78(438.9 kN/m) / 127.9 kN/m = 342.3 kN/m / 127.9 kN/m = 2.7

Analyze for 1 m of abutment length.

From Table B3-1, the loads and moments due to girders are

Under Group IV loads, the 25 percent overstress allowance can be applied to this allowable bearing pressure. By inspection, however, this computation is not necessary since q < qall, and the bearing stress is smaller than the allowable value. (OK)

Check sliding:

The forces, Fsliding, that tend to induce sliding are the sum of the following:

Shear loads from bearing pads, V (Table B3-1)

Active earth pressure load, PA (Table B3-2)

Horizontal earth load from live load surcharge, PLS (Table B3-2)

Analyzing per m of the abutment wall, Fsliding is

Fsliding = V/Lf + PA + PLS = 1047 kN/25 m + 69.96 kN/m + 16.02 kN/m = 127.9 kN/m

The force, FR, available to resist sliding (from Step 8) is

FR = 0.78(W + Pv)

The vertical force, Pv, computed above includes the self-weight of the footing, W. The live load should not be included in this calculation. Thus the factor of safety FS against sliding is

FSsliding = FR / Fsliding ≥ 1.5 (Eqn. 5-40)

[p. B-60] = 0.78(518.3 kN/m - 1538 kN/25 m) / 127.9 kN/m = 356.3 kN/m / 127.9 kN/m = 2.8

Again, the 25 percent overstress allowance could be applied, but since FS > 1.5, this is not necessary. (OK)

sections.body:
[p. B-64] The structural engineer has calculated the following values for loading along the abutment wall:

Loads at base of the superstructure (applied through the bearings at the girder seat) are summarized on Table B4-1.

[Table B4-1]

The shear load shown in Table B4-1 is the shear transferred through the bearings due to temperature, shrinkage and rib shortening. Under Group I loads, the load factor for this shear component is zero and will therefore not be included in the design loads for this example.

Final Service Load Design Loads for Group I:

Laboratory testing was limited to soil classifications and moisture content due to the granular nature of the soils encountered in the boring. The foundation design will be based largely on design parameters correlated to the soil classifications and the SPT N-values. sections.title: Example 4, Step 7 – Calculate allowable bearing capacity
sections.body:
[p. B-65] The geotechnical engineer will calculate the limiting allowable bearing capacity, considering both the potential for bearing capacity failure (Section 5.2) and settlement (Section 5.3).

Calculate Ultimate Bearing Capacity:

The general equation for bearing capacity is:

qult = cNcscbc + qNqCWqsqbqdq + 0.5γBfNγCWγsγbγ (Eqn. 5-14)

[p. B-66] The first term goes to zero since the foundation materials are granular and cohesionless, so the cohesion term, c, is zero.

The footing length (Lf) is 25 m. For footing widths (Bf) less than 5 m, the ratio of footing length, Lf, to width is greater than 5. This footing classifies as a strip footing, and the shape factors should be set equal to 1.0:

sγ = sq = 1.0 (Table 5-2)

Since this footing will be level, there is no effect of inclination of the base, so:

bγ = bq = 1.0 (Table 5-5)

Calculate the effect of the footing embedment, q. Assuming a 0.9-m-thick footing and 0.6-m cover, Df = 1.5 m:

In this case, q is only a function of the depth of bearing.

q = σ'vo = γ'Df where: γ' = γbulk = 19.6 kN/m³

q = (19.6 kN/m³)(1.5 m)

q = 29.4 kPa

[p. B-67] Since the ratio of the footing depth, Df, to the footing width, Bf, will be less than one, the correction factor to account for shearing resistance of the material above the bearing elevation, dq, should be set equal to 1.0:

dq = 1.0 (Table 5-4)

Check ground water effect:

Depth of ground water table below the bearing depth:

Df = Depth of footing = 1.5 m

Assumes a 0.9-m-thick footing and 0.6-m cover

Dw = Depth of ground water below the ground surface = 4.5 m

Conservatively estimate the footing width for ground water correction factors with an upper bound value of Bf = 6 m.

Calculate ground water correction factors, CWγ and CWq:

CWγ = 0.5 + 0.5(DW / (1.5Bf + Df)) ≤ 1.0 (Eqn. 5-9)

CWγ = 0.5 + 0.5(4.5 / (1.5(6) + 1.5)) = 0.7

CWq = 0.5 + 0.5(DW / Df) ≤ 1.0 (Eqn. 5-10)

CWq = 0.5 + 0.5(4.5 / 1.5) = 2.0 ; Use CWq = 1.0

A design friction angle associated with Unit 1a is needed to calculate the bearing capacity factors. From Figure B4-1, the average uncorrected SPT N-value for this unit is 22. From Figure B4-3, the average vertical effective stress in Unit 1 is 44.1 kPa (about 0.9 ksf). Entering Figure 4-1 with a blowcount of 22 and a vertical effective stress of 0.9 ksf, a relative density, DR, of about 85 percent is read. Entering Figure 4-2 with this relative density for well-graded sand (Unified Soil Classification ‘SW’), a friction angle of 38 degrees is selected for computing bearing capacity.

From Table 5-1, the bearing capacity factors, Nγ and Nq, are 78.0 and 48.9, respectively, for a friction angle of 38 degrees. So the equation for bearing capacity is:

[p. B-68] qult = 29.4 kPa (48.9)(1.0)(1.0)(1.0)(1.0) + 0.5 (19.6 kN/m³)(Bf)(78.0)(0.7)(1.0)(1.0)

qult = 1438 kPa + 535Bf

Incorporating a factor of safety of 3.0:

qall = qult ÷ 3.0

qall = (1438 + 535Bf kPa) ÷ 3.0

qall = 479 + 178Bf kPa

Estimate Footing Settlement:

First, estimate the settlement in the sand layers, 1a and 1b, assuming that settlement in the shale, Layer 2, will be negligible. Calculate stress increase at the midpoint of each soil layer using the 2-on-1 stress distribution method for various footing widths – say, Bf = 3.0, 4.3, 5.5 and 6.7 m:

ΔσV / q = Bf /(Bf + Z) (for strip footing) (Figure 5-12)

Layer 1a with midpoint of layer @ Z = 1.5 m below base of footing:

ΔσV1a / q = 3.0/(3.0 + 1.5) = 0.67

Layer 1b with midpoint of layer @ Z = 3.75 m below base of footing:

ΔσV1b / q = 3.0/(3.0 + 3.75) = 0.44

Perform similar calculations for Bf = 3.0, 4.3, 5.5 and 6.7 m, then tabulate as shown in Table B4-2.

[Table B4-2]

[p. B-69] Determine stress applied by footing to generate 25 mm of settlement for the same range of footing widths, Bf = 3.0, 4.3, 5.5 and 6.7 m, using the Hough method:

General equation:

ΔH = Ho(1/C') log[(σ'vo + Δσv)/σ'vo] (Eqn. 5-24)

Correct SPT blowcounts to account for overburden pressure, N′, for each layer, and enter Figure 5-19 to obtain bearing capacity factor, C′:

Layer 1a:

Navg = 22

N′/N = 1.47 (from Figure 5-18)

N′ = 32

C′ = 108 (from Figure 5-19 for well-graded sand and gravel)

Layer 1b:

Navg = 35

N′/N = 1.0 (from Figure 5-18)

N′ = 35

C′ = 115 (from Figure 5-19 for well-graded sand and gravel)

Calculate settlement in each layer and sum the settlements to obtain the total settlement under a range of applied stresses of q = 240, 290 and 335 kPa and a range of footing widths from 3.0 to 6.7 m:

Layer 1a:

ΔH1a = H1a(1/C') log[(σ'vo + Δσv)/σ'vo]

ΔH1a = 3 m(1/108) log[(58.8 kPa + 0.67(240 kPa))/58.8 kPa)]

ΔH1a = 0.0160 m = 16 mm (as printed; the terms give 0.0159 m)

Layer 1b:

ΔH1b = H1b(1/C') log[(σ'vo + Δσv)/σ'vo]

ΔH1b = 1.5 m(1/115) log[(95.6 kPa + 0.44(240 kPa))/95.6 kPa)]

ΔH1b = 0.004 m = 4 mm

∑ΔHi = 16 mm + 4 mm = 20 mm

Repeat and tabulate for various footing widths and applied stresses (a spreadsheet or other computer tool can make these calculations rapidly):

[p. B-70] [Table B4-3]

Check the estimated settlement in the shale, Layer 2, to verify that this settlement is negligible.

For settlement analysis, the shale can be modeled as elastic half-space. From elastic theory:

δv = CdΔσVBf(1 - ν²) / (αE EIR) (Eqn. 5-36)

αE = 0.0231(RQD) - 1.32 ≥ 0.15 (Eqn. 5-37)

From Table 5-12 for a rectangle with L/B ratio of 5, Cd = 1.83 (as printed; 1.83 is Table 5-12's Average value for L/B = 5, p. 97, where its Center value is 2.10; Example 5, p. B-89, takes the Center value for L/B = 3, and with 2.10 the settlement below is 0.0006 m). For a shale with RQD = 80%, ν = 0.14 and EIR = 9.8 x 10⁶ kPa, from Tables 5-13 and 5-14 (as printed; Table 5-13 gives shale a mean ν of 0.09, from 0.03 to 0.18). For a conservative footing width of 5.5 m and a bearing pressure of 290 kPa:

B = Bf + Z - Df = 5.5 m + 6.0 m - 1.5 m = 10 m

ΔσV = q(Bf/B) = 290 kPa(5.5 m/10 m) = 159 kPa

αE = 0.0231(80) - 1.32 = 0.53

δv = (1.83)(159 kPa)(10 m)(1 - 0.14²) / (0.53)(9800000 kPa) = 0.0005 m = 0.5 mm

This settlement is negligible.

Compare the values in Table B4-3 to allowable bearing capacities at the same footing widths relative to shear failure. Recall that the water table correction factor was conservatively computed near the upper bound of footing widths at Bf = 6 m. This would be revisited only if bearing capacity failure is found to limit the allowable bearing capacity.

For Bf = 3.0 m:

qall = 479 + 178(3.0 m) kPa = 1013 kPa >> 335 kPa (with 24 mm settlement)

[p. B-71] For Bf = 4.3 m:

qall = 479 + 178(4.3 m) kPa = 1244 kPa >> 290 kPa (with 24 mm settlement)

For Bf = 5.5 m:

qall = 479 + 178(5.5 m) kPa = 1458 kPa >> 290 kPa (with 25 mm settlement)

For Bf = 6.7 m:

qall = 479 + 178(6.7 m) kPa = 1672 kPa >> 240 kPa (with 23 mm settlement)

Settlement will therefore limit the allowable bearing capacity for the design of this footing. Interpolating the values in Table B4-3, find ranges of footing widths that will limit settlement to 25 mm or less at allowable bearing capacities of 240, 290 and 335 kPa:

sections.title: Example 4, Step 8 – Calculate sliding and passive soil resistance
sections.body:
[p. B-71] The geotechnical engineer has recommended that the footing be cast against the firm, undisturbed soil of Unit 1a. The friction angle of 38 degrees selected in Step 7 will be used to compute sliding resistance.

The general equation for sliding resistance is:

FR = (W + Pv) tan δ (Eqn. 5-38)

The second term goes to zero since we are founding the footing on a cohesionless soil unit. For a concrete footing cast against the ground, δ = φ, so the ultimate sliding resistance is:

FR = (W + Pv) tan 38° = 0.78(W + Pv)

Since the sliding resistance will develop at strain levels much lower than those needed to develop passive pressures against the side of the footing, passive pressure will be ignored unless it is [p. B-72] found that sliding resistance governs the design of the footing. The geotechnical engineer should provide this equation and the assumptions regarding use of passive pressures to the structural engineer for checking the footing’s resistance to sliding.

sections.title: Example 4, Step 9 – Check global stability of the footing
sections.body:
[p. B-72] The global stability of the abutment was checked using Bishop’s simplified method of slices using the slope stability computer program XSTABL™. For this analysis, the actual footing was modeled as a very strong material, thus forcing the critical failure surface behind the heel of the footing (i.e., failure surfaces that passed through the footing were not permitted). The output is shown in Figure B4-4.

sections.body:

• Subsurface profile at the interior bridge pier is shown in Figure B5-1.

[p. B-84] Solution:

The solution can be obtained by following the step-by-step process shown in Figure 6-1, Design Process Flow Chart.

Steps 1 through 4 – Preliminary bridge layout, review of existing geologic and subsurface data, site reconnaissance, scour and frost potential:

Given, Find, and Steps 1 through 4 (preliminary layout, existing data, reconnaissance, scour and frost); the calculation steps follow as their own sections.

sections.title: Example 5, Step 5 – Determine the loads applied to the footing
sections.body:
[p. B-84] The structural engineer has provided the loads applied at the base of the column as shown in Table B5-1.

[p. B-85] [Table B5-1]

Service Load Design Loads for Group VII:

The general equation is (refer to Example B-1 for discussion of variables):

PI = γ [βD(D) + βL (L + I) + βC(CF) + βE(E) + βB (B) + βS(SF) + βW(W) + βWL(WL) + βL(LF) + βR(R + S + T) + βEQ(EQ) + βICE(ICE)] (AASHTO, 1996, Eqn. 3-10)

Because the coefficients, β , for live load (L), impact (I), wind (W) and wind on live load (WL) are all zero for Load Group VII, this reduces to the following:

PVII = γ [βD(D) + βE (E) + βB (B) + βS (SF) + βEQ(EQ)]

Also, because there are no earth (E), buoyancy (B) or stream force (SF) loads in Table B5-1, the equation further reduces to:

PVII = γ [βD(D) + βEQ(EQ)]

The axial load due to earthquake can act in either the positive or negative direction. For checking bearing stress, the load will be considered to act downward. For checking overturning (eccentricity), the load will be considered to act upward. So the factored loads are as follows:

Axial loads for checking bearing stress:

Pv bearing = γ [βD(D) + βEQ(EQ)] = 1.0 [1.0 (6400 kN) + 1.0 (1671 kN)] = 8071 kN

[p. B-86] Axial loads for checking overturning:

Pv OT = γ [βD(D) + βEQ(EQ)] = 1.0 [1.0 (6400 kN) + 1.0 (-1671 kN)] = 4729 kN

Shear:

V = γ [βD(D) + βEQ(EQ)] = 1.0 [1.0 (167 kN) + 1.0 (804 kN)] = 971 kN

Moment about the Z-axis:

MZ = γ [βD(D) + βEQ(EQ)] = 1.0 [1.0 (211 kN-m) + 1.0 (1675 kN-m)] = 1886 kN-m

Moment about the Y-axis:

MY = γ [βD(D) + βEQ(EQ)] = 1.0 [1.0 (748 kN-m) + 1.0 (5546 kN-m)] = 6294 kN-m

sections.title: Example 5, Step 7 – Calculate allowable bearing capacity
sections.body:
[p. B-86] Allowable bearing capacities for footings on competent rock can be determined using presumptive bearing pressures. From Table 5-7, the recommended allowable bearing capacity for sound granite is 7.7 MPa. According to AASHTO (1996) Table 3.22.1A for earthquake loadings, the allowable bearing capacity can be increased by one-third, resulting in an overstress allowable bearing capacity under earthquake loads of 10.2 MPa; therefore, use qall = 10,200 kPa.

In general practice, settlement is not checked for Group VII loads because seismic loads are transient and temporary in nature. However, for completeness, we will check settlement in Step 10 based on elastic theory for the actual footing dimensions and bearing stress.
sections.applicability: Appendix B, Example 5 (an interior bridge pier on a spread footing on granite bedrock, sized for eccentricity under seismic moments; Service Load Design, Group VII (seismic) loads), printed heading Step 7 – Calculate allowable bearing capacity (p. B-86).

sections.title: Example 5, Step 8 – Calculate sliding and passive soil resistance
sections.body:
[p. B-87] The geotechnical engineer has recommended that the footing be cast against unweathered granite rock in Unit 2.

The general equation for sliding resistance is:

FR = (W + Pv) tan δ (Eqn. 5-38)

The second term goes to zero since we are not founding the footing on a cohesive soil unit. For a concrete footing cast against the ground, assume an interface friction angle of δ = 35 degrees (Table 5-15, after NAVFAC (1986b)). In reality, this is a very conservative assumption for mass concrete poured on a rough, monolithic rock surface. However, sliding is not usually the controlling condition for interior bridge foundations, so we will use this conservative assumption unless it is found to control the design of the footing. The ultimate sliding resistance is therefore:

Fsliding = (W + Pv)tan35° = 0.7(W + Pv) (as printed; this is the ultimate sliding resistance, FR in Step 11)

Since the sliding resistance will develop at strain levels much lower than those needed to develop passive pressures against the side of the footing, passive pressure will be ignored unless it is found that sliding resistance governs the design of the footing. The geotechnical engineer should provide this equation and the assumptions regarding use of passive pressures to the structural engineer for checking the footing’s resistance to sliding.

sections.title: Example 5, Step 10 – Size the footing
sections.body:
[p. B-87] The moments applied to the footing will create large eccentric loadings. First determine the minimum effective footing area necessary to provide sufficient bearing capacity. Then size the footing to account for the eccentric loading applied by the moment.

The minimum effective footing area is calculated as follows using the maximum axial load:

A′ = Pv bearing ÷ qall

A′ = 8071 kN ÷ 10,200 kPa = 0.79 m²

Due to the large differences in applied moments, make the footing rectangular to optimize the size. The relative dimensions of the footing should be the same as the relative magnitudes of the moments.

B′f = (L′f) MZ/MY = (L′f) 1886/6294 = 0.3(L′f)

[p. B-88] Determine the effective footing dimensions:

A′ = B′f × L′f

A′ = 0.3L′f × L′f

L′f = √(A′/0.3) = √(0.79 m²/0.3) = 1.62 m

B′f = 0.3(L′f) = 0.3(1.62 m) = 0.49 m

The actual footing dimensions are influenced by the eccentricity. Calculate the eccentricity using the minimum axial load.

ey = MZ ÷ Pv OT

ey = 1886 kN-m ÷ 4729 kN = 0.399 m

ez = MY ÷ Pv OT

ez = 6294 kN-m ÷ 4729 k (as printed, for kN) = 1.33 m

Determine the footing dimensions necessary to resist the moments by rearranging Equations 6-6 and 6-7:

Lf = L′f + 2ez = 1.62 m + 2(1.33 m) = 4.28 m

Bf = B′f + 2ey = 0.49 m + 2(0.399 m) = 1.29 m

Perform a quick check to ensure that overturning is also acceptable. Overturning will be acceptable if eccentricity in any direction is less than one-fourth the footing dimension in that direction for footings on rock, as discussed in Section 6.4.1.

(1/4)Bf = (1/4)(1.3 m) = 0.33 m < ey = 0.399 m (not OK)

(1/4)Lf = (1/4)(4.3 m) = 1.01 m (as printed; (1/4)(4.3 m) = 1.075 m) < ez = 1.33 m (not OK)

Therefore, use a minimum footing width and length of 4 times ey and ez, respectively.

Bf = 4ey = 4(0.399 m) = 1.6 m

Lf = 4ez = 4(1.33 m) = 5.32 m

Therefore, a footing with dimensions Lf = 5.4 m by Bf = 1.6 m will be stable and adequate for bearing capacity. Typically, the minimum footing width should be at least 3 column diameters [p. B-89] [i.e., 3(0.6 m) = 1.8 m] to provide the required development length for the reinforcement of the column-footing connection. The final dimensions of the footing will be controlled by the structural design of the footing, but the footing dimension should be no smaller than Lf = 5.4 m and Bf = 1.8 m.

Check the assumption regarding settlement:

Using elastic theory:

δv = CdΔσVBf(1 - ν²) / (αE EIR) (Eqn. 5-36)

αE = 0.0231(RQD) - 1.32 ≥ 0.15 (Eqn. 5-37)

From Table 5-12 for a rectangle with L/B ratio of 3, Cd = 1.78 (as printed; 1.78 is Table 5-12's Center value for L/B = 3, p. 97, where its Average value is 1.52, the column Example 4 reads on p. B-70; with 1.52 the settlement below is still 0.0003 m). For a granite with RQD = 100%, ν = 0.2 and EIR = 52 x 10⁶ kPa, from Tables 5-13 and 5-14 (as printed; Table 5-14 gives granite a mean EIR of 52.67 x 10⁶ kPa). The applied stress will be equal to the allowable bearing stress since the footing bears directly on the rock.

αE = 0.0231(100) - 1.32 = 0.99

So:

δv = (1.78)(10200 kPa)(1 m)(1 - 0.20²) / (0.99)(52000000 kPa) = 0.0003 m = 0.3 mm (as printed; the footing width found above is Bf = 1.8 m)

This settlement is negligible.

The design is acceptable for bearing capacity and settlement considerations.

sections.title: Example 5, Step 11 – Check overturning and sliding
sections.body:
[p. B-89] Overturning was already checked during the sizing of the footing in Step 10.

The footing will be stable against sliding if:

FS = FR / Fsliding ≥ 1.5

From Step 8:

FR = 0.7(W + Pv)

Calculate the weight of cover over the footing and the weight of the footing:

The footing is bearing 1.2 m below grade and can be assumed to be 1 m thick. [p. B-90] The area of the column is:

Acol = (π/4)(0.6 m)² = 0.28 m²

The weight of the footing and the soil cover is then:

Wftg = (1.0 m)(1.8 m)(5.4 m)(23.5 kN/m³) = 228.4 kN

Wcover = [(0.2 m)(1.8 m)(5.4 m) - (0.2 m)(0.28 m²)](19.6 kN/m³) = 37.0 kN

So, resistance to sliding is:

FR = 0.7(W + Pv OT)

FR = 0.7(Wftg + Wcover + Pv OT) = 0.7(228.4 kN + 37 kN + 4729 kN) = 3496 kN

The forces acting to cause the footing to slide are only due to the shear force, V, so

Fsliding = V = 971 kN

Then:

FS = FR / Fsliding = 3496/971 = 3.6

This should be greater than about 1.0 to 1.15 for seismic loads. (OK)
